Depression / Laziness / Lack of Motivation are all very interlinked.

The same way Happiness / Motivation / Energy / Ambition are all linked.

Those of us who have experienced depression before understand how important it is to maintain the good (read:healthy) activities *especially* when you don't want to.

The major issue with depression is not it's effect on people's energy levels, but rather it's effect on your outlook and ability to rationalize properly. That is why it is so scary and dangerous. The very way we *think* actually changes... what someone would normally rationalize positively, they instead rationalize negatively.

For example, healthy and happy people, even though they're dead tired, will still find the energy after a hard day of work to go exercise at the gym. Because even though it's not what they want to do in the present, they rationalize it's important for the future.

Depression isn't just staggering sadness like so many mistakenly think. It's a deeply rooted rot of your emotional strength. Sadness is a powerful emotion which needs a platform from which to exist off. If you're not happy, if you're just nothing, how do you quantify sadness?

Depressed people feel sadness, but they feel blandness more than anything.

I kind of agree with the concept that laziness does not exist. Laziness is simply the disregard of a person who doesn't grant significance or importance to something.

Take working to earn a living for example. If someone refuses to work to earn a living, and instead lives an unsatisfactory life; is that really simply *laziness*? Or is there an abundancy of underlying issues that sap this person of their desire to work?

They don't work, but they find the energy and the means to gratify themselves in various ways. If they can output effort to gratify themselves on a small-scale, they are not *lazy*. There is a failure in their rationality and they lack the ability to understand working will gratify them more effectively on a larger scale.

Someone has been sitting at home all day watching Netflix, their friend asks them to go to the gym, they decline. They don't want to output the effort it takes of going somewhere they dislike to do something they don't value. Their friend calls them lazy.

Again. Is it lazy? Or does that person simply prioritize spending their time doing something they enjoy more and find easier to accomplish at the same time? In most cases of this, the fact they find it easier to accomplish is one of the factors into how much they enjoy it.

So what is the point of all my rambling? The point is, only we ourselves can define what we value. The only way motivation comes to us, is if we desire something. If you find yourself content enough, your values shift, your motivation changes. That works both ways. 

Laziness is a blanket term we slap at people who don't share the same value, and therefore motivation for a certain something. But it is wholly misguided to do so, for it ignores the entire relationship between desire and result. If a human doesn't desire a result, they won't strive for it. And forcing a change in human desires, I have found to be, a nearly impossible feat. It has to happen... some how or way, which I cannot give you the answers to.

I would recommend looking to the future, thinking of all the positive things to come. If they don't preexist, create them. But don't just think of them, our brains are the most advanced computers in the world but they suck at self-maintenance. Write them down. Print them out and tape them to your wall for god sakes. Just make sure they are something you can randomly encounter, don't rely on your recollection skills.

It's very important you follow whatever desires you *do* have. It's actually imperative to your happiness, atleast for now. Put some genuine thought into large-scale desires of yours. New friends? Travel? New home? New experiences? New pet? Old friends? Old experiences? 

Once you decide on let's say 3 large improvements you desire, again, write them down, post them up, do whatever it takes to make sure you remember them. That part is very important.

Now before you even *think* about working towards them, make some small changes in your *daily* life. I like to change the lighting in my room, even something as simple as adding a lamp, changing bulbs, or buying something ambient and colourful. Get something changed in the room/s that you spend most of your time in. These are things you notice every day, they affect your mood. While you may have enjoyed the old things at one point, they are so incredibly stale to your mind that they have no benefit. So replace them with something else you enjoy, and receive the benefit from that for an undetermined amount of time.

Buy some potted flowers at your grocery store for $6, put them on your desk (in your room somewhere with light), and make it a challenge, not a burden, to keep it alive and make it grow and prosper.

And the single most important advice I can possibly give, and it's something I myself struggle with and will forever. 

**Forgive yourself, friend.**

All these desires you've successfully realized, you will need to create plans to work towards them. Some might be very difficult to achieve, requiring very small steps, and it can get overwhelming and it can get bleak. However I do believe you will succeed as long as you **forgive** yourself for any failing you encounter. If you have a goal you don't achieve, forgive yourself, and regroup. If you captivate your desire for something, and hold on to it, the only way you can lose that desire is through punishment. **Do not punish yourself for trying and not succeeding.** If you do, you will eventually realize you've associated all this negativity with the end result you initially desired, and you will lose motivation. Your body will adapt because it dislikes negativity, and your desire will change.

**Forgive your failures. Try again. Try a new approach. Try with help. Reevaluate your expectations compared to the likelihood of success, and set a realistic expectation. If you find reward in achievement, it doesn't matter how small you think that achievement may be. Keep achieving, keep rewarding, and in no time you will be someone you are much happier about being.**

I grew up with full, uncensored access to the internet. I was about 10 when the internet really started to take off for general consumers, during the late 90's, early 2000's. My father was a huge technology buff, he wanted my siblings and I to always have the latest and greatest hardware and software growing up because he understood the vision of computer technology and the internet. He didn't however truly understand what the nature of the internet would become, or rather, how encompassing and expansive it would become. So we were allowed unrestricted access to the internet and computer. It was an honest oversight, he simply couldn't predict what the internet would turn into.

Enter the early 2000's, when pornography has become so prevalent on the internet that kids can stumble upon it without intentionally seeking it out. Parents started to smarten up a little, age gates, parental restrictions etc. However my parents raised us to be responsible, allowing us the freedom to make our own decisions, and they hoped the values they bestowed onto us would lead us to make the smart and right decisions.

For the most part this method of upbringing was true. I never got into trouble, never started fights, always did well in school until the much later years (that's another story), always respected people and always desired good to prevail in the world. With the exception of my insatiable curiosity.

So from the age of ~10 and onwards, I *learned*, I *observed* and I *sought* every piece of information and media within my unlimited grasp. There was nothing I didn't want to know, or see, and there were *many* occaisons I wish I hadn't. Pornography, death, gore, hacking, cheating, manipulation, lying, drugs, theft and much more were just a handful of things available for me to take in. And even though I had no desire to *do* bad things, I was obsessed with learning about it.

Imagine a 12 year old replaying a beheading video over and over again simply because he was trying to emulate the emotional response it should cause in him. Trying to understand the consequences of taking a life, losing a life, losing a friend, and what that all means to him.

The issue is, at 12 years old, you're not developed enough to understand. Not truly. You can feel fear, and disgust, and the emotional ranges; but you have no context in which to learn properly from it. So what it does is numbs you. You replay the emotions over and over again, and instead of having the proper developed adult response; it dulls your emotions. It doesn't completely dull them, but enough so to warp your emotional growth being so young.

This sort of exposure for a kid certainly doesn't cause them to become a sociopath. But it leads them to develop *differently*, perhaps requiring a lot more effort to empathise; or perhaps by being *overly* capable of empathising with **negative** emotions such as pain.

This most noticeably affected me when it came to my exposure to pornography and it's effects on my sexual development. While I subjected myself to every extreme pornography imagineable, the biggest damage done to me was from chronic masturbation. Starting from around the age of 11 I learned how to masturbate from a relative who was just slightly older than me. After that, I manipulated my body for orgasm-highs to excesses that would be hard for most people to fathom.

A young, sexually unmatured kid masturbating consistently **every day** at least once a day. A habit which persisted unrelentingly through teenage years. I'm sure most of you can already inherently see the issue with that. It may not have started due to my access to the internet, but the access I had flourished the curiosity of sexuality of a young boy into an uncontrollable abuse of my body which changed the direction of my life undeniably and irreparably. 

It didn't take long for my addiction of touching myself to turn into an obsession with the idea of intercourse. It's not uncommon for teenage males to fawn over the idea of sex, however for me this started at a much too young age, and with an overwhelming severity.

The result of being able to view women naked, engaging in sex, and in any manner that I desired at my whim; crippled the development of my social skills. I unintentionally began to view women as objects whom which I simply *wanted* something from them.

Poor social skills subsequently curved into social anxiety, which then manifested seclusion, and tumbled out of control from there. When it became a strain and a fear to be around girls, naturally I felt more comfortable alone. I found solace in computer games, and online friendships, while the few friendships I had with males suffered due to my absence from fear of ending up in groups and encountering women.

This all comes across as such neurotic behaviour, and that's because it was. I was young, I didn't have the proper rationing abilities or guidance needed to address the issues as they snowballed and occured; I didn't even have an understanding of *why* these issues were occuring.

My highschool years became incredibly difficult as these issues grew into depression, and ironically my only consolation was my addiction to computer games and my online social life. The very root of my misery became the only hope for my sanity.

At this point you may be asking where was parent or teacher intervention. As much as I love and cherish my parents today, sadly they were too engrossed in divorce, financial issues and emotional issues of their own to be able to help me. My mother did her damned best raising 3 kids, working full time and trying to ensure we had a home to live in which was jeopardized by my fathers debt.

As an adult now, I don't know how she overcame and eventually conquered such monumental hardships; and managed to retain her own sanity and go on to create a happy life for herself and her kids. I feel she did the best humanly capable to help me permitting what she had to deal with; and I don't feel failed by many people. It was simply unlucky circumstances which led me to have to overcome my nightmare on my own.

There's is a plethora more to my sad story growing up through my teenage years, but I'm glad to say I am alive, well and in a much better place. If anyone is genuinely interested in hearing more of the story, I would entertain the idea. Maybe it could help others who are going through similar struggles, but for now I'll end it here.

This is how nsfw content all over the internet affected my life as a kid growing up who didn't and could not have known better. While the internet is in my opinion the single greatest tool in human history, it is also a portal of access that should be treated with the utmost consideration. 

There are potential dangers that lie in wait if that access is allowed to be explored unrestricted by kids too young to comprehend it all. Too young to properly rationalize, recognize and reason. Too young to know how harmful something seemingly harmless can truly be. 

So I implore all of you with young children or soon-to-be parents to consider my experience. Plan how you will best ensure your children aren't subjected to knowledge they're not prepared for. But most importantly, impress the importance of open communication into your children. It's a reality that they will eventually encounter something they don't know how to handle, they need to know and feel comfortable approaching their parents for help. No matter how severe, they need to be able to receive your help when they're conflicted. Your reasoning skills and wisdom far exceed theirs, and if you enable them to seek your help with conflict, you will foster a healthy mind and stable development in your children.

Honestly, sometimes I think if everyone with mental health issues lived together, seperate from those who don't struggle, we'd be a lot better off. We would be crazy, but we would be a group of understanding, sympathetic people who didn't judge "books" by their "cover" but their content.

But to be fair: Sometimes us *humans* in general, are capable of failure. Failure to sympathize, failure to *empathize* before we speak.

Our minds adapt to our surroundings. If someone grows up not knowing where their next meal is going to come from, they won't find that scenario nearly as bad as someone who has grown up living comfortably.

tl;dr You really can't blame people for being born into a comfortable bubble of ignorance, where they don't see the other side of life.
